General information: 
Unless otherwise noted, the chemicals and solvents were obtained from commercial 
sources and used without further purification. The reactions were monitored by thin-layer 
chromatography (TLC) with the products purified by column chromatography on silica gel 
(200-300 mesh, from Qingdao, China) if not noted otherwise. 1H NMR spectra were 
recorded at 400 MHz whi le 13C were recorded at 101 MHz with a Brucker ARX 400 
spectrometer. The chemical shifts (δ) are reported in ppm while the coupling constants (J) 
are reported in hertz (Hz). Tetramethylsilane was used as the internal standard for the 1H 
NMR spectra with a chemical shift at 0 ppm and CDCl3 as the solvent. CDCl3 was used as 
the internal standard for the 13C NMR spectra with a chemical shift at 77 ppm. The following 
abbreviations are used to symbolise the multiplicities: s = singlet, d = doublet, t = triplet, q 
= quartet, dd = doublet of doublets, td = triplet of doublets, dt = doublet of triplets, ddd = 
doublet of doublet of doublets, and m = multiplet. The HRMS data sets were obtained on 
Bruker Apex IV FTMS spectrometer (ESI) or ThermoFisher Hybrid Quadrupole -Orbitrap 
GC-MS/MS System Q Exactive GC (EI). 
 
Synthetic Procedures: 
4-Bromo-2,6-diisopropylaniline (compound S2): 
Compound S2 was synthesi sed by a modified method from the Weisenfeld ’s work 1. A 
solution of N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) (1.77 g, 10 mmol, 1.0 eq .) in N,N-
dimethylformamide (10 mL) was added dropwise over 30 min to a stirred solution of 2,6 -
diisopropylaniline (1.77 g, 10 mmol, 1.0 eq.) in N,N-dimethylformamide (20 mL) at 0°C. 
The reaction was stirred for another hour at 0°C, water (100 mL) was added. The resulting 
mixture was extracted with ethyl acetate and the combined organic layers were washed 
with saturated NH 4Cl solution (3 × 100 mL) followed by water (100 mL) and dried over 
anhydrous sodium sulfate. Solution concentration under vacuum afforde d 2.562 g 4 -
bromo-2,6-diisopropylaniline (compound S2) without purification, 99% yield. Compound 
S2 was used directly for the following step.

4

Compound S4 was synthesised according to Miyaura ’s work 2. A flask charged with 
PdCl2(dppf) (219 mg, 0.3 mmol), KOAc (1.47 g, 7 mmol), and B2pin2 (1.4 eq.) was flushed 
with nitrogen. DMSO (5 mL) and 3-(4-bromophenyl)propan-1-ol (1.08 g, 10 mmol, 1.0 eq.) 
were then added. After being stirred at 80°C for 24 h, the product was extracted with EtOAc, 
washed with water, and dried over anhydrous sodium sulfate and filtered with the filtrate 
concentrated in vacuo. Purification in a silica gel column (PE/EtOAc) afforded compound 
S4, 2.150 g, 82% yield. 1H NMR (400 MHz, chloroform-d) δ 7.74 (d, J = 7.4 Hz, 2H), 7.22 
(d, J = 7.4 Hz, 2H), 3.66 (t, J = 6.3 Hz, 2H), 2.72 (t, J = 7.6 Hz, 2H), 1.89 (p, J = 6.7 Hz, 
2H), 1.34 (s, 12H). This result corresponds to results in the literature3.

Macroscopic experiments of Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reaction: 
To prove the catalysis fact, we performed the macroscopic experiments of the catalysis of 
the molecular bridge in the same condition. The reaction indeed happened, which proves 
that the functional center of the molecular bridge works. The macroscopic reaction and 
result are presented as below.  
 
In a glove box, 4-bromotoluene (126 mg, 0.74 mmol), phenylboronic acid (90 mg, 1.0 eq.) 
and DMF (3.7 mL) were added to a Schlenk flask. After adding the molecular bridge (21 
mg, 3 mol%) and KO tBu (100 mg, 1.2 eq.) successively, the mixture was stirred at 65 oC 
for 24 h. Then, 50 mL ethyl acetate was added, washed with water three times. The organic 
phase was dried by Na 2SO4 and the solvent was removed under vacuum. The obtained 
residue was analysed by 1H NMR with adding 1,3,5 -trimethoxybenzene (10.7 mg) as 
internal standard. According to the literature report of the chemical shift of cross-coupling 
product6, the yield was determined as 27%. The yield of the macroscopic experiment was 
relatively low. The main reason was attributed to the side reaction between alkyl azide and 
palladium center7. During the catalytic process on the single -molecule platform, the side 
reaction does not exist and has no influence on the catalytic reaction. The cross-coupling 
product, 4-methyl-1,1'-biphenyl, was separated in a silica gel column (PE/EtOAc), and has 
been fully characterised by NMR spectra and high resolution mass spectra. 1H NMR (400 
MHz, Chloroform-d) δ 7.58 (d, J = 7.6 Hz, 2H), 7.49 (d, J = 7.7 Hz, 2H), 7.42 (t, J = 7.5 Hz,

7. Calculation of electron transmissi on and the pre -activation of the 
catalyst 
 
Figure S20 | Transmission spectra of four intermediates. a. Full transmission spectra 
of four intermediates. The transport device model was constructed by three parts, i.e. left 
electrode, central region and right electrode (Fig. S22). Both electrodes were semi-inﬁnite 
heavily p-type doped graphene (0.009 holes per carbon). The central region consisted of 
the extended molecule and one electrode extension on both sides. The structures of the 
transport devices were optimised using the B3LYP/6-31G(d)-LANL2DZ level of theory with 
Gaussian 09 software. The electronic transport simulations were performed by employing 
the real -space NEGF techniques 9,10 with GGA -PBE functional 11 and PseudoDojo 
pseudopotential, as implemented in the QuantumATK software (version: R-2020.09). The 
used basis sets were Medium for hydrogen, carbon and boron, High for nitrogen and 
oxygen, and Ultra for Palladium, respectively. The density mesh cutoff was set to be 125 
Ha. A k -point mesh o f 2×1×111 was used for device self -consistent calculations. The

38 
 
OzakiContour method is used for complex contour integration. The transmission spectra 
are calculated self-consistently for the bias voltage of 0.3 V with a k -point mesh of 12×1, 
based on which  the currents under bias 0.3 and 0.15 V are evaluated. The energy 
resolution for transmission spectra is set to be as high as 0.002 eV. The solvent effect is 
included. b. Enlarged transmission spectra of the four intermediates under a 0.3 V bias 
window. The current size is related to the position and size of the transmission peak in the 
bias window. State 1 has the smallest peak value and is the lowest state. The peaks of 
State 5 and State 4 are the largest, but only half of the transmission peak of State 4 is in 
the bias window, so State 5 is in the highest state, and State 4 is the second. The peak 
size of State 3 is between them. The transmission spectrum calculations are consistent 
with the conductance sequence of the four intermediates observed in experiments.

reaction was monitored in the solvent with 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% toluene

the number of catalytic cycles gradually decreased, which is consistent with macroscopic 
experiments.

increasing tol uene ratios show that the polarity decrease slows down the elementary

columns) has significantly faster growth relative to the other processes, which indicates 
that oxidative addition is more difficult at lower polarities.

Figure S28 | Time intervals of the four conductance states at various temperatures 
with single-exponent fits. As the temperature decreased, the dwell time and lifetime, τ, 
of each conductance state became longer, which means that the number of cycles per unit 
time decreased. In some low temperature cases at 285 K and 278 K, fewer catalytic cycles

Figure S29 | Rate constants for each elementary reaction at various temperatures.  
The maximum likelihood method was used to obtain the transfer rates between the four 
conductance states at various temperatures, which are presented as the forward (blue) 
and reverse (red) reaction rate constants between the four intermediates. The results show 
that as the temperature increased, both forward and reverse reaction rates between these 
states increased, which is consistent with activation energy theory. The transmetalation is 
the rate-determining step for the forward reactions. In addition, the reverse reaction rate 
constant for the reductive elimination is several orders of magnitude lower than the others, 
which indicates that the reductive elimination is less reversible.

Figure S3 5 | Dwell times of the conductance states in the forward reaction at 
different concentrations. Dependence of bimolecular reaction (oxidative addition (State

k=1/τ3) rates and independence of unimolecular reaction (transmetalation (State 4 to 5, 
k=1/τ4) and reductive elimination (State 5 to 1, k=1/τ5) rates on concentration. As the 
concentration increases, the dwell times of States 1, 2 and 3 approach the minimum value,

Table S4 | Dynamic and thermodynamic characteristics of single -molecule Suzuki-
Miyaura cross-coupling at different temperatures calculated f rom the I−t curves in 
Fig. 4a. 1，3， 4 and 5 in the title correspond to the conductance states 1, 3, 4 and 5. For 
the thermodynamic constants of every elementary reaction, we can acquire ∆G‡ at different 
temperatures through the Eyring equation ( k = (kBT/h) × exp(−∆G‡/RT)). The activation 
energy of each process is provided in Fig. 4f through the linear fitting of lnk versus 1000/T 
according to the Arrhenius equation (k = A×exp( −Ea/RT)). Then, ∆H‡ can be obtained by 
∆H‡ = Ea−RT and ∆S‡ = (∆H‡−∆G‡)/T. Finally, ∆G, ∆H and ∆S can be acquired through the 
difference between ∆G‡, ∆H‡ and ∆S‡ of the forward and backward reactions, respectively.

reaction according to the Hess's law.
